messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 74

David is fifty-five years old, single, and has worked as a counselor at a community mental health clinic for nearly twenty years. He takes a seat in my office on a Tuesday afternoon, his hands resting on his knees, perfectly still. He arrives early for every session, always on Tuesdays, because Wednesday is the anniversary of the shooting—and Tuesdays are the only days he can still drive himself here without pulling over to vomit.

Three years ago, on a gray November morning, David was in his office at the clinic, reviewing notes for his ten o’clock client. He heard a loud crack from the waiting room, then another, then a woman screaming. He froze. For a few seconds he did nothing—then he crawled under his desk and pressed himself against the wall, his hand over his mouth to quiet his breathing. He listened to more cracks, to footsteps, to the sound of a door being kicked in two doors down. He remembers thinking, *I am going to die. I am a counselor and I am going to die on this floor.* He stayed under the desk for what felt like an hour, though it was six minutes. When the police arrived and led him out, he saw a colleague from the front desk lying in the hallway. She was not moving. David tried to help, but an officer pulled him away.

That night, and every night for the next two months, he could not sleep without the lights on. He quit his job within a week. He told himself he needed a break, time to process. But the break stretched into a year. He moved to a smaller apartment with a deadbolt and a peephole and a security camera aimed at the front door. He stopped answering calls from friends. He began drinking, alone, in the dark, just enough to dull the edge before bed.

He eventually returned to counseling, but at a different clinic, one with a locked entrance and a buzzer system. His caseload is half what it used to be. He struggles with new clients who remind him of the ones he lost, or of the shooter—a former client he had discharged weeks earlier. He does not share this with anyone. He avoids the file room, because it looks like the hallway where his colleague died. He has a detailed evacuation plan for every room he enters. When a client becomes agitated, David feels his chest tighten and his vision narrow; he has excused himself mid-session twice, claiming a sudden headache, walking to the staff bathroom to splash water on his face until his hands stop shaking.

He tells me he is fine. He tells me his job is helping him heal. But he also tells me, in the same breath, that he can no longer watch news about shootings, that he changes the channel or leaves the room. He avoids loud noises, large gatherings, the sound of a chair scraping against a linoleum floor. He dreams of running, but his legs do not move, and he wakes with his heart pounding and a vivid, unbidden image of that November hallway.

Tonight, before our session ends, David looks at the clock. “Tomorrow is the anniversary,” he says, his voice flat. “I’ll stay home. I always do.” He stands, pushes his chair back carefully—silently—and walks to the door. He pauses. “I keep thinking I should have done something. That day. I was a counselor. I was supposed to help.” He does not wait for a reply. He leaves, and the door clicks shut behind him.
